raw_case_text: A 48-year-old man presented with high-grade fever with chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, acholic stools, dark urine, and yellowish discoloration of skin and sclera for one week. His past medical history was significant for diabetes and hypertension. He was immune to hepatitis A and B, with no history of bleeding diathesis nor recent use of new medications. He is a nonsmoker with no history of alcohol consumption. He returned from Pakistan 6 days prior to this admission. On presentation, the patient was ill-appearing, normotensive, and tachycardic (no relative bradycardia) but well perfused with diffuse abdominal tenderness and icteric sclera. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis and elevated creatinine. Liver function tests showed a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic picture, elevated ammonia levels, and negative hemolytic laboratory parameters (Table 1). Workups for viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic causes of hepatitis were negative, and serum salicylate levels were within normal range. Ultrasound of the abdomen revealed normal bile duct and gallbladder, and the absence of ascites. Doppler ultrasound ruled out thrombus. The echocardiogram revealed an ejection fraction of 61%-65%. A computerized tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed multiple liver cysts, mesenteric (Figure 1) and porta-hepatis lymphadenopathy (Figure 2), mild thickening of the terminal ileum (Figure 3) and proximal ascending colon. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed severe hepatic steatosis and multiple scattered liver cysts. Empirically ceftriaxone and metronidazole were initiated after obtaining blood cultures. Blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi. Intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone was continued. The patient clinically deteriorated on the above treatment and developed altered mental status, respiratory distress, and showed signs of ALF with an up-trending Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score. He was upgraded to the intensive care unit on Day 3 of admission, requiring on and off high-flow nasal cannula. His blood pressure remained within normal limits. Initially, IV ertapenem was started; however, the patient did not clinically improve and was not clearing the bacteria in the blood cultures, so the antibiotic was switched to IV meropenem on Day 5 of hospitalization due to its frequency of dosing and ability to achieve a comparatively better time to minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC), resulting in clinical recovery (creatinine improved, with hepatorenal syndrome ruled out) and clearance of infection on repeat blood cultures. The first blood cultures drawn grew Salmonella typhi resistant to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin. It was sensitive to azithromycin. No results were available for carbapenems. The patient completed 2 weeks of IV meropenem in-patient and was discharged after 22 days of hospital stay, stable on discharge, off any antibiotics, with negative blood cultures. One week after discharge, the patient was admitted due to back pain; however, his liver enzymes continued to remain within normal limits.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of high-grade fever with chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, acholic stools, dark urine, and jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high-grade fever with chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, acholic stools, dark urine, and yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclera for 1 week prior to admission. His symptoms began shortly after returning from travel to Pakistan 6 days before admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of diabetes mellitus and hypertension; documented immunity to hepatitis A and B; no history of bleeding diathesis. Returned from Pakistan 6 days prior to admission. Nonsmoker with no history of alcohol consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, acholic stools, dark urine, and scleral/cutaneous jaundice. Pertinent negatives: no recent use of new medications, no bleeding diathesis.

objective.physical_examination: On presentation, the patient was ill-appearing, normotensive, tachycardic (without relative bradycardia), and well perfused, with icteric sclera and diffuse abdominal tenderness. On hospital day 3, he developed altered mental status and respiratory distress.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed leukocytosis, elevated serum creatinine, a mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury pattern, elevated serum ammonia, and negative hemolytic parameters. Workups for viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic liver disease were negative, and serum salicylate level was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal bile duct and gallbladder without ascites, and Doppler ultrasound ruled out portal/hepatic vein thrombosis. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 61%-65%.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT revealed multiple hepatic cysts, mesenteric and porta-hepatis lymphadenopathy, and mild wall thickening of the terminal ileum and proximal ascending colon. MRCP demonstrated severe hepatic steatosis and multiple scattered liver cysts. Blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi resistant to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin and susceptible to azithromycin (carbapenem susceptibility not initially reported by the panel).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Extensively drug-resistant (ceftriaxone- and ciprofloxacin-resistant) Salmonella typhi bacteremia complicated by acute liver failure (ALF) with hepatic encephalopathy and acute kidney injury, confirmed by blood culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Viral, autoimmune, metabolic, toxic (salicylate), and vascular/obstructive hepatobiliary causes were ruled out. Empiric IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole failed to prevent clinical deterioration on day 3 (altered mental status, respiratory distress requiring ICU transfer and intermittent high-flow nasal cannula, and rising MELD score). Switching to IV ertapenem failed to clear bacteremia, prompting escalation on day 5 to IV meropenem (chosen for optimized dosing frequency and time above MIC). On a 2-week inpatient course of IV meropenem, the patient achieved full clinical recovery, normalization of renal function, and clearance of repeat blood cultures. He was discharged stable off antibiotics on hospital day 22; at a 1-week post-discharge visit for back pain, his liver enzymes remained normal.
